summary: In Greek mythology, the Logoi (Ancient Greek: Λόγοι, Lógoi) are the personifications of stories, tales, or words. They are counted among the children of Eris (Strife), born without a father, and are little more than abstractions whose identity is exhausted by the meaning of their name. Hesiod lists them in the Theogony immediately after their sibling Pseudea (Lies), and they are not notably personified anywhere else in Greek myth.
etymology: The name derives from the Ancient Greek common noun λόγος (lógos), "word," "speech," "account," or "tale"; the plural form Λόγοι (Lógoi) personifies the several stories or narrations they embody. The term is variously rendered "Tales," "Stories," or "Words."

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: The Logoi are listed by Hesiod in the Theogony (lines 226-232) among the offspring of Eris, the goddess of strife and discord, who was herself a daughter of the primordial Nyx (Night). According to this account Eris bears her children alone, with no father named.

Their siblings, the other children of Eris, include Ponos (Toil), Lethe (Forgetfulness), Limos (Famine), Algea (Pains), Hysminai (Combats), Machai (Battles), Phonoi (Murders), Androktasiai (Manslaughters), Neikea (Quarrels), Pseudea (Lies), Amphilogiai (Disputes), Dysnomia (Lawlessness), Ate (Ruin or Delusion), and Horkos (Oath).

sections.heading: Character
paragraphs: In Hesiod's catalogue the Logoi follow directly upon the Pseudea (Lies), and the two are often treated together as the deceptive and contentious aspects of speech. As personified abstractions the Logoi are regarded as little more than allegorizations of false or quarrelsome talk, with virtually no narrative or attributes beyond the sense of their name.
They are not notably personified outside the list of Eris's children, and no individual cult or distinct worship of the Logoi is recorded.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: As members of the brood of Eris, the Logoi belong to a group of personifications that embody the harmful and divisive forces in human life. Grouped with siblings such as the Neikea (Quarrels), Amphilogiai (Disputes), and Pseudea (Lies), they represent the wrangling and falsehood that strife brings into the world.
Personifications of this kind are characteristic of Hesiod's genealogy of evils, in which abstractions of conflict, deceit, and suffering are gathered together as the attendant offspring of Strife.
